'''''Bazemore v. Friday''''', 478 U.S. 385 (1986), is a [[Supreme Court of the United States|United States Supreme Court]] case in which the Court held that a [[regression analysis]] does not have to account for every possible factor that could influence salary in order to be considered as evidence of discrimination.<ref name=":0">{{ussc|volume=478|page=385|pin=|year=1986}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |date=1986 |title=Bazemore v. Friday: Salary Discrimination under Title vii |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1341151 |journal=Harvard Law Review |volume=99 |issue=3 |pages=655–667 |doi=10.2307/1341151 |jstor=1341151 |issn=0017-811X|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Norris |first=Barbara A. |date=1986 |title=Multiple Regression Analysis in Title VII Cases: A Structural Approach to Attacks of "Missing Factors" and "Pre-Act Discrimination" |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.2307/1191650 |journal=Law and Contemporary Problems |volume=49 |issue=4 |pages=63–96 |doi=10.2307/1191650 |jstor=1191650 |issn=0023-9186|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Background ==

The case of ''Bazemore v. Friday'' originated from a lawsuit filed by black employees of the [[North Carolina Agricultural Extension Service]], a public agency providing [[agricultural education]] and services.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cooperative Extension Serving People – a Brief History |url=https://www.ces.ncsu.edu/cooperative-extension-serving-people-a-brief-history/ |access-date=2023-07-09 |website=www.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref> The plaintiffs alleged that the agency was practicing racial discrimination in its salary decisions, violating [[Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964]].<ref name=":0" /> The agency had previously operated separate programs for black and white employees, and although it had integrated the programs, it continued to pay the black employees less than their white counterparts.

== Lower Courts' Decisions ==

The District Court and the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit|Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals]] initially ruled in favor of the defendant, stating that the plaintiffs had failed to prove that the salary disparities were due to racial discrimination. The courts argued that the plaintiffs' regression analysis, which was used to demonstrate the [[Racial pay gap in the United States|wage gap]], was insufficient because it did not account for all possible factors influencing salary.<ref name=":0" />

== Supreme Court Ruling ==

The case was then appealed to the Supreme Court. In a unanimous decision, the Court reversed the lower courts' rulings.<ref name=":0" /> The Court held that a [[regression analysis]] does not need to include every conceivable variable to be admissible as evidence of discrimination. The Court stated that the plaintiffs had met their burden of proof by showing a significant disparity in pay between black and white employees, and that the defendant had failed to provide a non-discriminatory explanation for this disparity.

[[William J. Brennan Jr.|Justice Brennan]] delivered the opinion of the Court.<ref name=":0" />

== Impact and legacy ==

The decision in ''Bazemore v. Friday'' has had a significant impact on [[Employment discrimination law in the United States|employment discrimination]] lawsuits. It has clarified the standards for statistical evidence in such cases, making it easier for plaintiffs to prove discrimination.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fairley |first1=William B. |last2=Huber |first2=William A. |date=2018 |title=Statistical Criticism and Causality in Prima Facie Proof of Disparate Impact Discrimination |journal=Observational Studies |volume=4 |issue=2 |pages=11–16 |doi=10.1353/obs.2018.0001 |s2cid=258609217 |issn=2767-3324|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Gastwirth |first=Joseph L. |date=2020-03-09 |title=The Role of Statistical Evidence in Civil Cases |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev-statistics-031219-041238 |journal=Annual Review of Statistics and Its Application |language=en |volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=39–60 |doi=10.1146/annurev-statistics-031219-041238 |bibcode=2020AnRSA...7...39G |s2cid=211430271 |issn=2326-8298|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The case has been cited in numerous subsequent court decisions and has influenced the development of employment law in the United States.<ref name=":1" /><ref>[https://scholarship.law.vanderbilt.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1803&context=faculty-publications Joni Hersch and Blair Druhan Bullock, The Use and Misuse of Econometric Evidence in Employment Discrimination Cases, 71 Washington & Lee Law Review. 2365 (2014)]</ref>
